learn.title: Let the program check itself
learn.body: An assertion is a claim you make in code: this must be true here. If it is false, the program stops at once and tells you which claim failed, instead of carrying a wrong value onward.

learn.title: assert in action
learn.body: `assert` comes from the header `assert.h`. All three claims hold, so it prints `all passed`. A false one would stop the program with a message naming the expression, file and line.

learn.title: When it fails
learn.body: A failing `assert` prints something like `Assertion failed: (twice(5) == 11), file a.c, line 7` and aborts. The exact wording depends on your system. Build with `-DNDEBUG` and every assert is removed.

learn.title: Choose good test cases
learn.body: Test a normal case, then the edges: zero, a negative number, the biggest and smallest allowed value. Bugs like to hide at the edges. Write the expected answer by hand first, not by running your code.

learn.title: Test a function
steps: Add one assert per case and run after every change

learn.body: Use assert for your own mistakes, not for checking user input, which must always be handled.

questions.explanation: A true assertion has no visible effect.

questions.prompt: What happens when an assertion is false?
choices: The program stops with a message
questions.explanation: The message names the expression, the file and the line.
Include the header `assert.h` to use it.

questions.prompt: Which flag removes every assert from the build? Type it.
Which test is an edge case for `twice`?
questions.explanation: Zero sits at the boundary between positive and negative.

questions.prompt: Where should you get the expected answers for your tests?
choices: Run the code and copy its output
Work them out by hand first
questions.explanation: Copying the output only proves the code agrees with itself.

questions.prompt: Match each test to what it checks.
questions.explanation: Good tests cover normal, edge and odd inputs.
